title: Here's What 2 Weeks of Vacation Taught Me About Leadership
author: Gaurav Jain
summary: Writing from his own experience of fully disconnecting from a team of managers and senior technical leaders for two weeks, the author reports returning not to a backlog of delayed decisions but to a team that had handled escalations, production issues and even a blameless postmortem without him. He uses that surprise to interrogate the manager's belief that constant availability keeps projects on track. Ten lessons follow, but the throughline is that his over-involvement had served his own need for control more than the team's needs. He distinguishes delegating tasks from delegating authority, argues that a leader's real value lies in strategy and talent development rather than daily operations, and treats absence as a way to surface future leaders. The conclusion reframes switching off as a trust signal: a leader who never disconnects tells the team, without meaning to, that he does not trust them.
points: The author concedes that his frequent check-ins may have reflected his own need for control rather than any operational necessity.
His budget analogy captures the key distinction: delegating tasks without authority is like handing someone a budget while keeping the purse strings tight.
Stepping back is presented as a talent-spotting tool, since those who rise to the occasion in a leader's absence reveal the leadership pipeline.
He proposes a blunt success metric for leaders - how well the team performs when you are not there
and calls making oneself redundant the aim of leadership.
The closing reframe is that failing to switch off on vacation unintentionally signals distrust to the team.
quotes: Before diving into the lessons learned, let me set the stage. I’ve been leading a team of smart professionals for several years now, including managers, senior technical leaders, and their extended teams. We’ve worked hard to build a culture of trust, belonging, and open communication.

Even though I had shared my phone number so they could reach me during emergencies, nobody called. The team promptly took care of the customer escalations and production issues that came up during the time and even conducted a blameless postmortem (which I was quite impressed with).
Lesson: Building a foundation of trust is crucial. When team members feel trusted, they’re more likely to take initiative, make decisions, and handle challenges independently.

This experience demonstrated the importance of delegating authority, not just the tasks. By being unavailable, I had unintentionally given my team the authority to make decisions — and they handled it admirably.

Lesson: Periodically create opportunities for team members to lead, even when you’re not on vacation. It can reveal hidden talents and future leaders, and automatically build up your leadership pipeline.
In fact, the best leaders are always in pursuit of making themselves redundant. That is the holy grail of leadership.
Trust is the foundation for building a great team that can perform at their best. But when don’t switch off, we unintentionally signal to our team that we don’t trust them.
